title: Blood for blood
summary: The Hebrew is a perfect six-word mirror (shofek dam ha-adam / ba-adam damo yishafek). The form enacts the content: the act returns on its doer.

title: The flood narrative as a single mirror

summary: Wenham showed that the flood story, often divided by critics into two sources, reads as one carefully balanced structure turning on 'God remembered Noah' (8:1). Even the numbers mirror: 7 days, 40 days, 150 days — 150, 40, 7.

title: Created in His image
summary: The Hebrew runs created–man–image / image–God–created–him (vayyivra … betsalmo / betselem … bara oto), so the line turns on the image at its centre; a third clause follows outside the mirror.

title: The Abraham cycle as a mirror

levels.label: C
levels.text: Sarai in a foreign palace; Abram and Lot part

levels.label: E
levels.text: Covenant with Abram; annunciation of Ishmael

levels.label: E'
levels.text: Covenant with Abraham; annunciation of Isaac

levels.label: D'
levels.text: Abraham comes to the rescue of Sodom and Lot

levels.label: C'
levels.text: Sarah in a foreign palace; Abraham and Ishmael part

summary: Eleven chapters fold around the covenant of Genesis 17, where Abram becomes Abraham (17:1–5 is the focal point in Rendsburg's outline). Each episode before it has a partner after: two genealogies, two journeys of faith that begin 'go' (lekh lekha, 12:1 and 22:2), two wife-in-a-foreign-palace stories, two rescues of Lot. Rendsburg's handout prints C as 12:1–13:18, overlapping B; the palace episode itself begins at 12:10, which is used here.

summary: Fishbane showed the Jacob stories folding around the births of Jacob's children (focal point 30:22–25: Rachel gives birth, and Jacob resolves to go home). Angels meet Jacob as he leaves the land (28:12) and as he returns (32:1); he flees Esau and later comes back to face him; both interludes set a matriarch or daughter in a foreign ruler's house.

title: Measure for measure

levels.label: A
levels.quote: whether he is a foreign resident or native;

levels.label: B
levels.quote: And if a man takes the life of anyone else, he must surely be put to death.

levels.label: C
levels.quote: Whoever kills an animal must make restitution—life for life.

levels.label: D
levels.quote: whatever he has done must be done to him:

levels.label: X
levels.text: Fracture for fracture, eye for eye, tooth for tooth
levels.quote: fracture for fracture, eye for eye, tooth for tooth.

levels.label: D'
levels.quote: Just as he injured the other person, the same must be inflicted on him.

levels.label: C'
levels.quote: Whoever kills an animal must make restitution,

levels.label: B'
levels.quote: but whoever kills a man must be put to death.

levels.label: A'
levels.quote: the same standard of law for the foreign resident and the native;

summary: The law of retaliation is set at the centre of a mirror that also enacts it: each case returns in reverse order, as the penalty returns on the offender. The frame insists the same law binds the foreign resident and the native. Welch extends the pattern to the narrative around it (vv. 13–14, 23).

title: Ephraim and Judah
summary: The Hebrew names Ephraim, Judah, Judah, Ephraim: the northern and southern kingdoms enclose each other, the reconciliation drawn in the word order.

title: The key of David
summary: Open–shut–shut–open (patach / sogher / sagar / potheach). Revelation 3:7 applies the saying to Christ.

title: My thoughts, your ways
summary: The Hebrew runs my thoughts–your thoughts–your ways–my ways; verse 9 then restates the contrast with the heavens above the earth.

title: Two masters

levels.label: B'
levels.quote: or he will be devoted to the one

summary: Hate–love, then devoted–despise: rejection encloses attachment, and either way one master loses. The Greek keeps the same order.

title: Find and lose

summary: Find–lose–lose–find. The saying recurs across the Gospels with 'save' in place of 'find' (Matthew 16:25, Mark 8:35, Luke 9:24, 17:33).

title: Judgement without favouritism

levels.label: A
levels.quote: will repay each one according to his deeds.

levels.label: B
levels.quote: To those who by perseverance in doing good seek glory, honor, and immortality, He will give eternal life.

levels.label: C
levels.quote: But for those who are self-seeking and who reject the truth and follow wickedness, there will be wrath and anger.

levels.label: C'
levels.quote: There will be trouble and distress for every human being who does evil, first for the Jew, then for the Greek;

levels.label: B'
levels.quote: but glory, honor, and peace for everyone who does good, first for the Jew, then for the Greek.

levels.label: A'

summary: Paul frames the passage with impartial judgement (vv. 6, 11), sets reward for doing good at both inner edges (7, 10) and wrath for evil at the centre (8–9). Grobel identified it as a retribution formula built as a chiasm.

levels.label: A

levels.label: B
levels.text: Eating with tax collectors and sinners

levels.label: C
levels.text: The question about fasting: the bridegroom taken away

summary: Dewey showed Mark's five opening conflicts arranged concentrically: two healings frame the section, two stories about eating sit inside them, and the centre gives the first hint of Jesus' death, when the bridegroom is taken away (2:20). The section ends with the first plot against him (3:6).
